strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful problem: distributional optimization over large discrete scientific design spaces can be much more efficient when the objective has exploitable decomposable structure.

DADO is a conceptually appealing synthesis of EDAs, factorized search distributions, and junction-tree message passing. The exposition generally builds useful intuition from fully decomposable cases to soft decompositions.

The method is evaluated on both synthetic decomposable functions and protein-property-predictor objectives, and the reported gains over a similarly parameterized decomposition-unaware EDA are often large.

The paper includes substantial derivational detail and appendices, including links to classical message passing, entropy-regularized variants, and additional ablations over sample budget and protein datasets.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is too narrow for a top-tier acceptance threshold. The main baseline is essentially only a naive EDA; the paper does not compare against Factorized Distribution Algorithms, Bayesian optimization with additive/factor graph structure, evolutionary methods, gradient-free optimizers, or exact/classical message-passing where tractable.

The protein experiments optimize and evaluate using the same learned proxy objective, so they mainly demonstrate proxy optimization rather than scientific design quality. There is no wet-lab validation, no independent oracle, and limited analysis of oracle exploitation or whether high-scoring generated sequences remain reliable under the predictor.

The synthetic setting is limited: only one random function per sequence length in the main text, tree decompositions with singleton nodes, and no systematic variation of graph topology, factor size, decomposition misspecification, or objective ruggedness. This makes it hard to assess robustness beyond the favorable setting.

There are technical ambiguities in the Monte Carlo estimation of the distributional value functions. The algorithm description appears to reuse joint samples in a way that does not clearly estimate child expectations conditional on each parent assignment, and the indexing in Algorithm 1 is confusing enough to raise reproducibility and soundness concerns.

The paper does not sufficiently quantify computational tradeoffs. DADO uses many factor models and message computations; runtime, memory, wall-clock cost, and scaling with junction-tree width are not compared against baselines.

The claim of broad applicability to scientific design is stronger than the evidence. The paper assumes a useful decomposition is available or learnable, but the practical procedure is only lightly explored and can fail for cases such as intrinsically disordered proteins.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone: important implementation details of junction-tree construction, component-function parameterization, message estimation, and code availability are not fully specified.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful problem: distributional optimization over large discrete scientific design spaces can benefit from known decomposable structure in the objective.
The proposed DADO algorithm is conceptually intuitive, combining factorized search distributions with message-passing-style value propagation over a junction tree.
The manuscript is generally readable and provides a substantial derivation, including connections to EDAs, policy optimization, and classical graphical-model message passing.
Experiments consistently show that DADO can outperform a decomposition-unaware EDA when the objective is explicitly decomposed and the provided decomposition is favorable.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is too narrow for a top-tier AI acceptance. The main baseline is essentially only a naive EDA; the paper does not compare against stronger or more directly relevant methods such as classical/max-product optimization when feasible, factorized distribution algorithms, genetic/evolutionary methods using linkage, simulated annealing/MCMC, BO variants for decomposed functions, or modern policy-gradient/CEM-style alternatives.

The experimental setup strongly favors the proposed method. Synthetic objectives are generated from exactly the structure given to DADO, often with singleton tree nodes, and only one random landscape per sequence length appears to be used. Significance tests over random seeds on a fixed landscape do not establish robustness across problem instances.

The protein experiments do not convincingly demonstrate scientific design utility. The methods optimize learned surrogate models and report surrogate scores, without experimental validation, independent oracle evaluation, uncertainty handling, or a strong check that optimized sequences remain in-distribution or biologically plausible.

The paper explicitly brackets off objective-model error, but this is central to real scientific design. Since the method can exploit inaccuracies in a decomposed surrogate, the main practical claims are stronger than the evidence supports.

Theoretical development is not fully satisfying. The transition from exact message passing to the proposed stochastic weighted-MLE updates relies on approximations and lower-bound arguments, but the paper provides limited guarantees about monotonic improvement, convergence, bias/variance of the sampled value estimates, or conditions under which DADO improves over standard DO.

There are clarity and possible correctness issues in the algorithmic presentation. For example, the value-function estimation pseudocode appears ambiguous or incorrectly indexed, and it is not clear how conditional expectations are estimated for arbitrary parent assignments under finite samples.

Computational fairness is underexplained. DADO uses many local factors and message computations over the decomposition, while the naive EDA uses a single autoregressive model; the paper does not clearly compare wall-clock cost, parameter counts, component-function evaluations, or equalized compute budgets.

The real-data decompositions are obtained by thresholding AlphaFold-predicted residue distances, a crude heuristic whose accuracy and sensitivity are only lightly explored. The paper does not establish that this decomposition is reliable across protein classes, especially for disordered or conformationally flexible proteins.

Hyperparameter selection appears optimistic: learning rate and shaping temperature are swept separately per method and per objective and selected based on final optimization performance, which may overstate attainable performance in realistic use.
The claimed generality to arbitrary decompositions and broad scientific design domains is not matched by the evaluation, which is almost entirely synthetic plus protein-surrogate optimization.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and important opportunity: many scientific design objectives have decomposable structure, but standard distributional optimization/EDA methods do not exploit it. The proposed DADO framework is well motivated and relevant to protein and other discrete design settings.

The technical idea is appealing: factorizing the search distribution according to a junction tree and using message-passing-style value functions to coordinate local weighted maximum-likelihood updates. The derivation connects classical max-product/message passing, EDAs, and entropy-regularized policy optimization in a coherent way.

The empirical results consistently support the main qualitative claim. On synthetic decomposable landscapes, DADO improves substantially over a decomposition-unaware EDA, with the gap increasing for larger sequence lengths. On protein-derived predictive models, DADO is usually better and otherwise comparable.

The paper includes useful ablations in the appendix, including sample-budget comparisons and a study of the contact-distance threshold controlling decomposability. These strengthen the case that decomposition quality matters in the expected way.

The writing is generally clear for a technically involved paper, and the authors provide enough implementation detail, hyperparameter sweeps, datasets, and a reproducibility statement to make the work relatively easy to follow and likely reproducible.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies almost entirely on comparison to a naive decomposition-unaware EDA. Given the related work discussion, stronger baselines are needed: factorized distribution algorithms, Bayesian-network EDAs, exact/dynamic-programming optimization where tractable, BO-style decomposed optimizers, and relevant policy-optimization variants would make the empirical claim much more convincing.

The protein experiments optimize learned decomposed predictors rather than validating designed sequences against true experimental measurements or even systematically against held-out ground truth. This limits the strength of claims about scientific design utility, especially because model exploitation is a known failure mode in offline design.

The learned protein predictors are central to the experimental claims, but their predictive quality is not reported prominently in the main results. Without clear holdout metrics for each protein and threshold, it is hard to know whether DADO is finding genuinely promising sequences or simply exploiting artifacts of the decomposed surrogate.

The synthetic experiments are somewhat narrow: the main setting uses tree decompositions with singleton nodes and randomly sampled pairwise components. This is useful for controlled validation but does not fully stress the junction-tree machinery with larger cliques, approximate decompositions, misspecified decompositions, or non-treewidth-trivial cases.

The paper would benefit from a more explicit computational complexity and wall-clock/runtime analysis. DADO uses many factor networks and message-passing computations, and it is not clear when the statistical efficiency gains outweigh the overhead relative to simpler EDAs or exact message passing.

Some algorithmic details are potentially ambiguous, especially around Monte Carlo estimation of distributional value functions, baselines/mean-shifting, and the exact weighting/shaping used in practice versus the derivation. These details matter for reproducing and understanding the method’s stability.

The main claims are sometimes broader than the evidence. The method plausibly generalizes to many scientific design domains, but the empirical support is limited to synthetic landscapes and protein-property surrogate optimization. The paper should frame non-protein applications more cautiously.

strengths: Clear and interesting algorithmic contribution: the paper extends EDA-style distributional optimization to decomposable discrete objectives using junction-tree factorization and message-passing value functions, which is a natural but nontrivial synthesis of EDAs, graphical models, and policy optimization ideas.
The method is well motivated for scientific design problems where sparse interactions are plausible, and the exposition gives useful intuition before the formal derivation.

Empirical results are directionally convincing: DADO consistently improves over a naive EDA and other included baselines on synthetic decomposable landscapes, with gains increasing for larger sequence lengths, and shows promising results on several protein-property proxy optimization tasks.

The appendix is substantial, with derivations, baseline details, dataset descriptions, robustness studies for decomposition choice, additional protein cases, and runtime measurements. The paper appears more reproducible than many submissions, assuming the referenced code is available.
weaknesses: The evaluation is still somewhat narrow relative to the claims about scientific design. The protein experiments optimize learned decomposed proxy models rather than validating designs against true assays or even stronger independent predictors, so the practical impact for real design remains only indirectly supported.

The main empirical setup gives DADO a favorable structural match: the objective itself is constructed to obey the junction-tree decomposition used by DADO. This is appropriate for testing the method, but it leaves open how much benefit remains when the true objective only approximately decomposes or when the decomposition is misspecified in more realistic ways.

Baselines are incomplete for a top-tier AI venue. Comparisons are mainly to EDA/FDA/PPO variants; stronger discrete optimization and model-based design baselines such as genetic algorithms, CEM variants, simulated annealing/local search, GFlowNet-style methods, or Bayesian optimization acquisition optimizers would make the empirical case much stronger.

The theory is mostly an algorithmic derivation rather than a rigorous guarantee. The lower-bound/value-function argument is plausible but does not establish convergence, monotonic improvement, approximation error behavior, or conditions under which the estimated value-function updates are reliable.

The method depends critically on having or learning a useful decomposition, but decomposition discovery is largely outside the contribution. The AlphaFold/contact-threshold heuristic is reasonable for proteins, yet may not transfer broadly, and the paper could better delimit where DADO is expected to work.

Some reported results suggest limitations that are not fully resolved: in larger-node protein junction trees, FDA can outperform DADO, and the authors attribute this to value-function variance without a deeper diagnostic or remedy. This weakens the claim that message passing is consistently the key advantage.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: distributional optimization over large discrete scientific design spaces when the objective has exploitable decomposable structure.
weaknesses: The practical impact is not convincingly established because the protein experiments optimize learned surrogate models rather than experimentally validated designs or reliable ground-truth fitness; this leaves open whether DADO finds genuinely good biological sequences or merely exploits the fitted decomposed predictor.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and technically meaningful algorithmic contribution: a decomposition-aware distributional optimization method that combines factorized search distributions with message passing over a junction tree. The connection between classical max-product/message-passing optimization and EDA-style weighted maximum-likelihood updates is well motivated.

The method is positioned well against relevant baselines, especially naive EDA and FDA, which helps isolate the value of both factorization and message-passing-based local weights. Including PPO-style updates as an additional baseline is also useful.

The empirical results are consistently favorable on synthetic decomposable landscapes, with evidence that the gap grows with sequence length and remains under larger alphabets. These experiments support the central intuition that exploiting decomposability improves sample efficiency in high-dimensional discrete design.

The protein experiments make the work more compelling than a purely synthetic contribution. Using AlphaFold-derived contact graphs, several real protein assay datasets, and decomposed learned property predictors gives a plausible path toward practical scientific design.

The appendix is substantial and includes derivations, dataset details, baseline descriptions, robustness studies for decomposition graphs, and runtime measurements, all of which improve reproducibility and help clarify the assumptions.
weaknesses: The real-world evidence is still indirect: the protein experiments optimize learned decomposed predictors rather than experimentally validated designs or even independently validated optimized candidates. This leaves open whether DADO improves actual scientific design outcomes rather than exploitation of the chosen surrogate models.

The strongest protein results are on datasets selected partly because their AlphaFold-derived junction trees have small nodes. Additional datasets with larger nodes are relegated to the appendix and show weaker or mixed advantages, including cases where FDA can outperform DADO. This limits the breadth of the empirical claim.

The objective functions in the protein experiments are constructed to obey the decomposition used by DADO. This is methodologically coherent, but it makes the evaluation somewhat self-referential: the paper does not fully test performance when the true oracle has substantial interactions outside the assumed junction tree.

The theoretical development is intuitive and useful, but the paper does not provide strong convergence, approximation, or sample-complexity guarantees for the proposed stochastic updates. Several choices, such as shaping functions, baselines, one gradient step, and resampling frequency, remain heuristic and empirically tuned.

The comparison to broader model-based optimization and protein design methods is limited. The paper compares optimization algorithms on fixed objectives, but does not benchmark against stronger end-to-end design pipelines that handle surrogate uncertainty, priors, or model exploitation, which are important in realistic settings.

Reproducibility is mostly good in terms of experimental detail, but the reproducibility statement appears to mention public GitHub code without a visible URL in the manuscript text, and full practical replication would depend on implementation details for junction-tree construction and decomposed predictor fitting.
